The Brazilian codling (Urophycis mystacea) attains a maximum total length of 66.5 centimeters [Li = 66.5 centimeters], a value derived from extensive trawl surveys along the continental shelf. Females in this population reach the onset of puberty at a total length of 43.9 centimeters [Lp = 43.9 centimeters], which corresponds to an estimated age of approximately 4.5 years based on otolith-derived growth records. The maximum reproductive output for this species has been estimated by drawing on fecundity-length relationships established for the closely related white hake (Urophycis tenuis), with a weight correction applied for size differences. At a sustained water temperature of 15.8 °C [T = 15.8 °C], females are capable of producing roughly 1 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 1 million eggs per spawning event] across multiple spawning events. This annual fecundity figure reflects the species' iteroparous life-history strategy and its adaptation to relatively cool, productive waters where extended spawning seasons are common among gadiform fishes.

Newly hatched larvae of the Brazilian codling emerge from pelagic eggs with a wet weight at birth of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a mass calculated from the typical egg diameter of 0.76 millimeters observed across several Urophycis species. This minute neonatal mass necessitates an immediate reliance on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding, which occurs within the first week following eclosion. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults reaches 1380 grams [Wwi = 1380 grams], a figure derived from the length-weight relationship W = 0.00295 × L³·¹¹ applied to the asymptotic total length. This dramatic increase in body mass, spanning over six orders of magnitude from the larval to the adult stage, underscores the species' capacity for rapid somatic growth during the juvenile phase. The pronounced ontogenetic shift in body size also correlates with changes in habitat use, as larvae drift in pelagic waters while larger juveniles and adults transition to demersal, benthic environments.

Reproductive maturation in female Brazilian codling occurs when individuals reach a wet weight of 378 grams [Wwp = 378 grams], corresponding to the body mass at the onset of puberty derived from the same length-weight relationship applied to the length at puberty. This threshold mass represents a critical developmental milestone, after which resources are increasingly directed toward gamete production rather than solely toward somatic growth. Field surveys indicate that females at this body weight are undergoing active vitellogenesis and possess developing oocytes, confirming the transition to reproductive competence. The energetic investment required to reach this mass, which is approximately one-quarter of the ultimate adult weight, likely demands several years of consistent foraging on benthic crustaceans and small fish. In comparison to confamilial species with similar maximum sizes, this pubertal mass appears consistent with a moderate pace of maturation that balances early reproduction against continued somatic expansion.

The maximum lifespan of the Brazilian codling has been estimated at approximately 4380 days [am = approximately 4380 days] under the prevailing thermal conditions of its habitat, a value derived from captive and mark-recapture studies conducted at 15.8 °C [T = 15.8 °C]. This longevity, corresponding to roughly 12 years, places Urophycis mystacea among the longer-lived members of its genus and aligns with its relatively delayed maturation and moderate reproductive output. Age validation using otolith thin sections has confirmed annulus formation and supports a maximum recorded age of 12 years in wild individuals. The species' extended lifespan is characteristic of demersal fishes inhabiting cool-temperate waters, where slower metabolic rates and reduced predation pressure on adults contribute to increased survival. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in condition factor and a reduced capacity for annual spawning, although some females remain reproductively active well into their tenth year.

Among the Urophycis species, Brazilian codling exhibits a female length at puberty of 43.9 centimeters [Lp = 43.9 centimeters], representing approximately 66 percent of the ultimate total length of 66.5 centimeters [Li = 66.5 centimeters], a ratio that suggests a conserved allometric scaling pattern within the genus. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 378 grams [Wwp = 378 grams] is roughly 27 percent of the ultimate wet weight of 1380 grams [Wwi = 1380 grams], a disparity that reflects the nonlinear nature of the length-weight power function. Such size-based metrics are routinely used in fisheries stock assessments to estimate spawning biomass and to set minimum size limits for commercial harvest. The species' modest neonatal mass of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams] and the protracted lifespan of approximately 4380 days [am = approximately 4380 days] at 15.8 °C [T = 15.8 °C] position the Brazilian codling as a slow-growing, relatively long-lived species with a conservative reproductive strategy.
